title: Materials Around Us
intro: Look around you — every object is made of some material, and each material has properties that decide what it can be used for. This chapter teaches you to observe materials, group them, and understand why we choose one material over another.

sections.heading: What Things Are Made Of
bullets: Every object is made of one or more materials — a chair may have wood, metal, and cloth.
Common materials around us are wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper, cloth, rubber, leather, and stone.
The same object can sometimes be made of different materials — chairs, mugs, and toys can be wood or plastic or metal.
We pick the material based on what the object has to do.

sections.heading: Properties: How Materials Behave
bullets: Appearance: shiny (metals), dull (wood, paper).
Hardness: a hard material doesn't bend easily; a soft material does (sponge vs glass).
Transparency: see-through (clear glass), translucent (oily paper), opaque (wood).
Floating or sinking in water: leaf floats, iron nail sinks.
Solubility: sugar dissolves in water (soluble), sand does not (insoluble).
Magnetic or non-magnetic: iron is magnetic, wood is not.

sections.heading: Grouping Materials
bullets: Materials can be grouped by their properties so they're easier to study.
Soluble vs insoluble: salt and sugar dissolve; chalk powder and oil do not (oil instead floats).
Floats vs sinks: a wooden block floats, a steel spoon sinks.
Transparent (clear glass), translucent (frosted glass), and opaque (cardboard) describe how light passes through.
Different people may pick different ways to group, and that's fine — each grouping is useful for a different purpose.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Material
bullets: Cooking pots are made of metal because metal can stand high heat without melting or burning.
Window panes are made of glass because we need to see through them.
Raincoats and umbrellas use plastic because plastic doesn't let water through.
Schoolbags use cloth or strong synthetic fabric because they need to be light, strong, and washable.
We pick a material by matching its properties to the job.

sections.heading: Some Special Properties
bullets: Lustre: the shine of a freshly cut metal — gold, silver, iron all have lustre.
Conductivity: metals let heat and electricity flow through them; wood and plastic don't.
Flexibility: rubber bends and returns to shape, while glass cannot.
Brittleness: clay pots break suddenly when dropped.
These properties decide which jobs a material is suited for.

sections.heading: Materials and Our Environment
bullets: Some materials, like paper and cloth, decay easily and return to nature.
Plastics last for hundreds of years and harm soil and water if thrown away.
We can reduce harm by following 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' — use less, use the same item again, and put waste into the right bin.
Carrying a cloth bag instead of taking a plastic one is a small but useful step.
Choosing materials wisely is about both today's job and tomorrow's earth.

key_takeaways: Every object is made of one or more materials with their own properties.
Properties include hardness, transparency, floating/sinking, solubility, and magnetism.
Materials are grouped by properties to make them easier to study and use.
We choose materials by matching their properties to the job — metal for pots, glass for windows.
Lustre, conductivity, flexibility, and brittleness are properties that often decide use.
Reduce, reuse, and recycle to limit harm to the environment, especially from plastics.

glossary.definition: The substance from which an object is made — wood, metal, plastic, etc.
A feature of a material, like hardness or transparency, that helps describe it.
Lets light pass through fully so we can see clearly through it (clear glass).
Lets some light through, but you can't see clearly (oily paper).
Does not let light pass through; we cannot see through it (wood).
A substance that dissolves in a liquid (sugar in water).
A substance that does not dissolve in a liquid (sand in water).
The shine on the surface of a freshly cut metal.
A material that lets heat or electricity flow through, usually a metal.
To turn used material into new objects so it isn't wasted.
